name: Aisha Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the pension credit team at the benefits office near the bus station. It's top-up money for older people on low incomes, so most of my claimants are in their seventies or eighties. I do phone calls in the morning and a few booked appointments in the afternoon, going through bank statements and savings, which is fiddly. I'm still learning the capital rules, and I get the calculations wrong more often than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The people. A lot of them have been too proud to claim for years, and you can hear how hard it was to pick up the phone. One lady brought me a tin of shortbread after her award came through. At home it's me and my partner Jonas, he's an electrician. We've got a decent chunk saved, mostly in index funds, because Jonas's dad drilled it into him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's more or less what I expected, if I'm honest. The tools we've got now are fine but nothing special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small ways and people on both sides got a bit carried away. At work I'd probably say the call summaries save me ten minutes a day. I'm not one to post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the job stays and I get time to actually get good at it. I'd still be the one doing the sums on someone's savings. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Use the call summary tool when it's reliable, ask Mohammed on my team to check my capital sums until I've got them. And keep the monthly amount going into the index funds with Jonas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, honestly. Job's safe, money's fine, Jonas is busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the call summaries now and then. Do you trust them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. It gets the gist of a call right. But the call summary tool once wrote that a man's wife had died when the man had said his dog had. So I read every summary before it goes on the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any bigger plans in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably look at buying in a year or two. Nothing in this picture changes that. Jonas wants a garage for his van.

say: AI is **useful in small ways**; both sides got carried away.
The **call summaries** save me about ten minutes a day.
think: The job stays, and I get time to **get good at it**.
I'll still be the one doing **the savings sums**.
do: Use the **call summary tool** only when it's reliable.
Ask Mohammed to **check my capital sums** for now.
Keep **monthly payments** into the index funds.
S0.quote: The call summary tool once wrote that a man's wife had died when the man had said his dog had.
fieldNote: She's **pragmatic**: notes the small benefit, dismisses the hype.
A **funny error** keeps her reading every summary.
**Savings and Jonas's trade** make home life feel secure.

steps.text: Read every AI call summary before it goes on the file
Keep paying into the index funds every month with Jonas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's more real. Our whole team is checking and answering, so that would land on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change the job and we should be sensible about it. Keep people where people matter, use the tools for the paperwork. I wouldn't be marching, but I'd want a straight plan from management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd stop hiring juniors, and the older staff would retire and not be replaced. I'm junior, so I'd be on the edge. With my calculation errors, I'm not top of the keep list if there's a cut on the pension credit team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the tools are tested and the others are using them, I'd learn them properly so I'm not behind. I'd ask to move to the home visits team, because a lot of older people need someone in the room. And I'd stop the index fund top-ups for a while and keep more as cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel I could do something, but I'd be checking the internal job board every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The claimants who can't use a phone, let alone a chatbot. And Mohammed, who's fifty-two and been on pension credit for twenty years. He's brilliant at it but he can't type fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the household cope if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still be fine. Jonas is out wiring houses, and that's hands-on, so it lasts longer. It's more about what I do every day than about the bills.

say: **Keep people** where people matter; tools for paperwork.
I'd want a **straight plan** from management, not marches or angry posts.
think: They'd **stop hiring juniors**, and I'm on the edge.
My **calculation errors** keep me off the keep list.
do: **Learn the tools** once they're tested by others.
Ask to **join home visits** for older claimants.
**Pause fund top-ups** and hold more as cash.
S1.quote: With my calculation errors, I'm not top of the keep list if there's a cut on the pension credit team.
fieldNote: She waits for **proof** before learning tools, then commits.
Her move is toward **home visits**, people-facing work.
Her partner's **trade job** steadies household money, so the worry is about her days.

steps.text: Learn the new claims tools once colleagues have tested them
Apply to join the home visits team for older claimants
Pause index fund top-ups and keep more cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's hard to take in. Everything I do is in my head or on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope the government and the companies slow down a bit, because people aren't ready. Not stop it, but slow it. I'd say it to friends, maybe sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone by 2029. The pension credit work is rules and sums, and a machine that's better than a person at that doesn't need me. The only bit left might be sitting with someone in their living room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd look at training for something with my hands and people, like an occupational therapy assistant, fitting rails and helping older people at home. That gets me to about 2031 before robots. I'd keep the savings, not touch the funds, and I'd hold off on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. I'd be awake doing maths about how long we'd last on Jonas's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would you last on Jonas's money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not long without cuts. Maybe a year and a half with savings. But then his job meets robots three years later. My partner Jonas and I would both be in the same boat, just staggered three years apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change anything about your plans together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd wait. We'd talked about getting married next summer. I'd still want to, but small, not the big do his mum wants.

say: Government and companies should **slow it down**, not stop it.
I'd **sign a petition** and say people aren't ready.
think: My **job's gone** by 2029, because pension credit is rules and sums.
The only bit left is sitting in a **living room** with an older claimant.
do: Train as an **occupational therapy assistant** for home work.
**Hold off** on the house and keep the savings.
Have a **small wedding** instead of a big one.
S2.quote: My partner Jonas and I would both be in the same boat, just staggered three years apart.
fieldNote: She sees both jobs going, **staggered** by the robot gap.
Her move is to **hands-on care** for older people.
She'd shrink the **wedding** rather than cancel it.

steps.text: Train as an occupational therapy assistant at the college
Hold off buying a house until both jobs look clearer
Sign the petition asking government to slow AI in benefits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Not good, but better. I could see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to plan, and I'd ask my manager what the department's plan is for juniors. With friends I'd say don't panic, but don't sit still. I'm not going to be the one posting doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the job still goes, just in 2031. But I'd have time to finish training without rushing, and Jonas's work has until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for a year or two and use the tools as they come in, because that's sensible. In year two I'd start the occupational therapy assistant course part-time. We'd buy a small house, because Jonas's income is steady for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you more or less sure about the occupational therapy idea with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More, I think. In the fast one I'd rush and probably pick wrong. Here I could try a few shifts with the home adaptations team before I commit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop putting effort into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rules, honestly. Learning the capital rules feels a bit pointless if a machine does it in five years. But it's still my job until then, and I want to do it right.

say: It's **time to plan**: what's the department's plan for juniors?
**Don't panic**, but don't sit still either; I won't post doom.
think: The job still **goes in 2031**, just a bit later.
I'd have time to **train without rushing** while Jonas works until 2034.
do: **Use the tools** as they arrive at work.
Start the **OT assistant course** part-time in year two.
**Buy a small house** while Jonas's income is steady.
S3.quote: In the fast one I'd rush and probably pick wrong.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan into **tested steps**.
She'd **try shifts** before committing to a new career.
She keeps doing **the job right** even if it's ending.

steps.text: Use the new AI tools on pension credit cases as they arrive
Start the occupational therapy assistant course part-time in year two
Buy a small house while Jonas's wiring work is steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time and we should use it calmly. At work I'd be the one saying 'let's learn this properly'. Not doom, not hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job's safe for a good while. I'd get good at the casework, then decide. I'd be more worried about Mohammed than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next year, get married, and keep at the job. I'd learn the AI tools once they're properly in use. Around year five I'd look seriously at the home visits or OT route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but it's far enough off that I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about children differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. We'd want one in the next five years anyway. Ten years of notice means I'm not making the decision about children scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. Jonas and I would keep the funds going. That's what they're for.

say: There's time, so we should **use it calmly** and steadily.
I'd be the one saying **'let's learn this properly'**.
think: The job's **safe** for a good while, so I can get good at casework first.
I'd worry more about **Mohammed**, fifty-two, than about me.
do: **Buy the house** next year and get married.
**Learn the AI tools** once they're properly in use.
Look at the **OT route** around year five.
S4.quote: Ten years of notice means I'm not making the decision about children scared.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **keep life plans** on track.
Her worry shifts to an **older colleague**.
She'd still **keep saving** the way she always has.

steps.text: Buy a house with Jonas next year as planned
Learn the pension credit AI tools once they're in use

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Both our jobs go, just three years apart, and two years isn't enough to train for anything. What would help is a paid course for people like me to move into care and home support, and some honest dates from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably about the older people. Half my claimants don't have email. If everything moves to a machine, someone still needs to sit at their kitchen table with them.

headlineQuote: Half my claimants don't have email.
portrait: A **27-year-old pension credit caseworker**, still learning the capital rules and making calculation errors.
She uses AI **now and then**, mostly call summaries she always reads through.
**Savings in index funds** and her electrician partner make home life feel secure.
She'd move towards **hands-on care** for older people as AGI gets closer.
With more time she **keeps life plans**: house, wedding, maybe children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both jobs go, three years apart.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** to move into care and home support.
